\title{When Does Edge AI Defect Inspection Pay Back Its Carbon? Measured Embedded Inference, Detector Recall, and Alert Design}

\author{Utkarsh~Sengar%
\thanks{U.~Sengar is with the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Dharwad, Karnataka 580011, India (e-mail: cs23bt026@iitdh.ac.in).}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Edge AI inspection is often assumed to be green because it prevents scrap; critics point to the electricity of always-on inference. We test both claims with a conservation-checked accounting model comparing four edge-AI alert policies with no inspection and manual inspection, using measured or sourced inputs: the power of a real PatchCore pipeline at 30~FPS on an embedded \JetsonModel{} (\JetsonFullTotalPower~W for the whole module) and on a workstation GPU, the recall of two detectors on all \DetCategories{} MVTec~AD and VisA categories, alert rates from our companion alarm-management study, and public life-cycle data. Compute never decides: the edge cell accounts for at most \EdgeOfBenefitMax\% of the benefit, and replacing the embedded module by a workstation changes the outcome by at most \PlatformDeltaCMax\%. Against no inspection, edge AI wins in every Monte Carlo draw of three reference scenarios, and the analysis reduces to one rule: inspect when the defective parts produced per hour carry more embodied carbon than the cell emits per hour, about \NomogramGramsPerHour~gCO$_2$e. Against human inspectors the outcome hinges on recall. At a strict alarm-budget threshold, PatchCore's median recall is \DetPcMvtecRecallMedian{} on MVTec~AD but \DetPcVisaRecallMedian{} on VisA; edge AI then beats manual inspection in only \McProbLMin--\McProbLMax\% of draws, and detector recall explains \RecallSobolMin--\RecallSobolMax{} of the variance. Carbon-optimal thresholds restore the advantage, saving up to \HiValOptSavingCapMax~\kgce{} per 1{,}000 high-value parts without extra reviewers. Alert design matters too: single-frame alerting needs tens to hundreds of reviewers, and on slow lines reviewers who distrust mostly-false alerts can erase the benefit.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Sustainable manufacturing, edge AI, industrial anomaly detection, energy measurement, carbon accounting, alarm management, uncertainty analysis.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{A}{utomated} optical inspection with unsupervised anomaly detectors such as PatchCore and PaDiM~\cite{roth2022patchcore,defard2021padim} is now accurate enough on public benchmarks~\cite{bergmann2021mvtec} for deployment on edge computers beside production lines. Two opposing sustainability narratives surround these deployments. One holds that inspection is intrinsically ``green'' because intercepted defects are reworked instead of scrapped. The other, prompted by the rapid growth of machine-learning energy use~\cite{strubell2020energy,desislavov2023trends}, asks whether always-on inference erodes those gains. Neither claim is usually quantified for an actual production line, and published estimates rarely separate measured quantities from assumptions. A third factor is usually left out: a detector that alerts on every frame can bury the operators who must act on its alerts.

We ask three questions for a functional unit of 1{,}000 inspected parts:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Magnitude.} How large is the measured electricity and embodied-hardware footprint of an edge inference cell relative to the material, rework, workload and field-escape effects that inspection changes?
\item \emph{Counterfactual.} Against which baseline---no inspection or manual end-of-line inspection---and under which defect prevalence, compute budget and grid intensity does edge AI stop being carbon-beneficial?
\item \emph{Policy.} With identical compute, how do measured alert policies change operator workload and carbon, and how much recall may temporal filtering lose before it stops paying off?
\end{enumerate}

This paper makes four contributions:
\begin{itemize}
\item An open, conservation-checked accounting model with explicit counterfactual baselines (no inspection, manual inspection) and four AI alert policies, driven by one validated parameter ledger (Tables~\ref{tab:parameters} and~\ref{tab:policies}) whose provenance classes are reported (\RegistryMeasuredCount{} measured, \RegistryPaperACount{} imported from our alert-policy study, \RegistryLiteratureCount{} literature, \RegistryOfficialCount{} official dataset, \RegistryAssumptionCount{} scenario assumptions).
\item Measured inputs instead of assumed ones: line-rate power of a real PatchCore pipeline on an embedded module (whole-module power) and on a workstation GPU, with a protocol that respects the refresh limits of on-board sensors~\cite{yang2024accurate}; and per-part recall and false-positive rates of two detectors on all \DetCategories{} categories of two public industrial benchmarks.
\item A closed-form decision rule, $\pi\beta>k$, equivalently a throughput-free break-even chart, validated on a population of \PopSize{} sampled products and complemented by break-even frontiers, PRCC and Sobol sensitivity, and a weight-robust multi-criteria index. It shows that detector recall, not compute, decides the comparison with human inspection.
\item Three links between alarm management and sustainability: alert policy dominates operator load, temporal filtering pays off only within a quantified recall-loss margin, and carbon-optimal detection thresholds differ sharply from conventional alarm budgets; in addition, reviewer distrust of unreliable alerts (the cry-wolf effect) can erase the benefit on slow lines.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\emph{Industrial anomaly detection.} MVTec~AD~\cite{bergmann2021mvtec} established the standard benchmark; PatchCore~\cite{roth2022patchcore} and PaDiM~\cite{defard2021padim} use pretrained CNN patch features with nearest-neighbour or Gaussian scoring. Our earlier work benchmarks cost-calibrated thresholding~\cite{sengar2026flagship1}. A companion study~\cite{sengar2026paperA} turns PatchCore scores into operator alerts through exponential smoothing, $k$-of-$N$ persistence, machine-state gating, divergence triage and an incident latch, and measures eight policy variants on simulated inspection workloads. On good parts, single-frame thresholding raised \PaperAFaRaw{} false alerts per hour and the full policy \PaperAFaFull{}; a sustained defect produced \PaperAPerDefectRaw{} alerts under thresholding and \PaperAPerDefectFull{} under the full policy, at a mean delay of \PaperADelay{} frames. We import those per-policy measurements, with their confidence intervals, and the study's reviewer service rate.

\emph{Energy of machine learning.} Energy accounting for ML has concentrated on training and data-centre inference~\cite{strubell2020energy,henderson2020towards,desislavov2023trends}. On-board NVIDIA sensors are convenient, but on some architectures they sample only part of the runtime, and they refresh at limited rates~\cite{yang2024accurate}. Long, steady-state measurement windows mitigate both problems.

\emph{Manufacturing material and energy efficiency.} Material production dominates the energy of many products~\cite{gutowski2013energy}, and material efficiency---including yield improvement and scrap avoidance---is a recognised mitigation lever~\cite{allwood2011material,ashby2012materials}. ISO~14040/14044 standardise life-cycle assessment practice~\cite{finkbeiner2006new}. Human visual inspection typically misses 20--30\% of defects~\cite{see2012visual}; this range bounds our manual baseline. We know of no work that places measured edge-inference energy and measured alert loads on the same functional unit as these quality-driven flows.

\section{Accounting Model}
\subsection{Functional Unit, Regimes and Boundary}
The functional unit (FU) is $N=1{,}000$ consecutively produced parts. A line with throughput $\Theta$ [parts/h] needs $T_{FU}=N/\Theta$ hours to produce one FU. The gate-to-gate boundary (Fig.~\ref{fig:boundary}) covers inspection electricity, operator-review or manual-inspection workstations, rework electricity, the embodied carbon of unrecovered scrap, the processing burden of recovered scrap, the amortised embodied carbon of the edge hardware, and the consequences of field escapes. Facility base loads, logistics of good parts and labour-related emissions are identical across regimes, so we exclude them. The study is a comparative assessment organised along the goal-and-scope elements of ISO~14040/14044~\cite{finkbeiner2006new}. Its question---what changes when a line adopts a given inspection regime---is consequential, so only flows that differ between regimes enter, and all results are differences between regimes rather than absolute footprints. Recovered scrap is modelled as closed-loop recycling: it replaces virgin material one-to-one and carries only its processing burden $EF_{rec}$, so the full material factor applies to the unrecovered share. Electricity carries average, location-based grid factors. Consequential studies often prefer marginal factors, which can differ substantially from average ones~\cite{hawkes2010marginal,silerevans2012marginal}; instead of committing to one, we report the grid intensity at which each conclusion reverses (Section~\ref{sec:breakeven}).

Six regimes enter the comparison. \emph{N0}: no inspection. \emph{L0}: 100\% manual end-of-line visual inspection with recall $r_{L0}$, discovery delay $d_{L0}$ and $t_{L0}$ seconds per part. \emph{B0--B3}: a continuously running edge AI cell under one of the four alert policies measured in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}: single-frame thresholding (B0), exponential smoothing (B1), smoothing with $k$-of-$N$ persistence (B2), and the full policy, which adds an incident latch, machine-state gating and divergence triage (B3). The cell diverts flagged parts automatically and an operator reviews every alert afterwards, so review queues do not delay interception.

\subsection{Defect Routing and Reworkability}
With prevalence $\pi$ the FU contains $D=N\pi$ defects in classes A (reworkable), B (scrap-prone) and C (escape-sensitive) with shares $f_A,f_B,f_C$. A regime with recall $r$ and interception delay $d$ [s] yields
\begin{align}
N_{rw} &= f_A\, r D\, q_{rw}(d), \quad q_{rw}(d) = q_0\, e^{-d/\tau_{rw}}, \label{eq:rw}\\
N_{sc} &= rD - N_{rw}, \qquad N_{esc} = (1-r)D, \label{eq:sc}
\end{align}
where $q_0$ is the zero-delay reworkability and $\tau_{rw}$ the time constant with which a defective part advances into irreversible downstream operations. By construction $N_{rw}+N_{sc}+N_{esc}=D$, and the implementation checks this identity numerically at every evaluation. For L0, $r=r_{L0}$ and $d=d_{L0}$. For an AI policy $t$, $d=d_t/f_{cam}$ with the measured mean delay $d_t$ in frames, and $r=r_{AI}-\delta_r$, where $r_{AI}$ is the detector's recall and $\delta_r$ is a recall loss charged only to the persistence policies B2 and B3. The companion study observed no such loss---all four policies detected every sustained defect---so $\delta_r$ is centred on zero and studied as a break-even parameter.

\subsection{Material, Workload and Energy}
Scrap mass is $M_{gr}=N_{sc}m$ for part mass $m$, of which $M_{rec}=\eta M_{gr}$ is recovered and $M_{loss}=(1-\eta)M_{gr}$ lost. We adopt the operator-load model of~\cite{sengar2026paperA}: every alert reaches the review queue. For policy $t$ the false-alert rate is $\lambda_{FA}=\lambda_t+g\,b_t$, where $\lambda_t$ [1/h] is the measured rate on good parts, $b_t$ the measured alerts per glare burst and $g$ [1/h] the rate of glare bursts. Each detected defect raises $a_t$ alerts. The operator therefore reviews $n_{ev}=\lambda_{FA}T_{FU}+a_t\,rD$ alerts per FU, giving
\begin{equation}
H = \frac{n_{ev}\, t_{review}}{3600}\ \text{[h/FU]}, \qquad \rho = \frac{n_{ev}\, t_{review}}{3600\, T_{FU}},
\end{equation}
where $t_{review}$ [s] is the time to review one alert and $\rho$ is the utilisation of a single operator; for L0, $H=N t_{L0}/3600$ and $\rho=\Theta t_{L0}/3600$; for N0, $H=0$. Electricity per FU [kWh] is
\begin{align}
E_{edge} &= (P_{idle}+P_{active}+P_{host})\,T_{FU}/1000, \\
E_{rev} &= H\,P_{station}/1000, \qquad E_{rw} = N_{rw}\,e_{rw},
\end{align}
with $E_{edge}=0$ for N0 and L0. $P_{idle}$ and $P_{active}$ are the measured idle and above-idle power of the edge computer at the camera rate (Section~\ref{sec:measure}); $P_{host}$ covers what the measurement cannot observe: the carrier board, camera and lighting of the embedded cell, and in addition the host computer when a workstation GPU is used.

\subsection{Carbon}
Carbon per FU is the sum of seven non-negative components,
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
C ={}& M_{loss}EF_{mat} + M_{rec}EF_{rec} + \gamma\,(E_{rw}+E_{rev}+E_{edge}) \\
& + C_{hw}T_{FU}/L_{hw} + N_{esc}\,(m\,EF_{mat}+c_{ret}) \\
& + \kappa f_C N_{esc}\, m\,EF_{mat},
\end{split}
\end{equation}
where $EF_{mat}$ is the cradle-to-gate material factor, $EF_{rec}$ the processing burden of recovered scrap, $\gamma$ the grid intensity, $C_{hw}$ and $L_{hw}$ the embodied carbon and service life of the edge computer (the hardware term, like $E_{edge}$, is zero for N0 and L0), and each escaped part is replaced (its material is lost) and shipped back, with return and replacement road freight $c_{ret}=2\,(m/1000)\,d_{ret}\,EF_{fr}$ at GLEC intensities $EF_{fr}$ [kgCO$_2$e/t-km]~\cite{glec2023}; class-C escapes add collateral damage $\kappa\, m\,EF_{mat}$. Escape consequences scale with the part; they are not a fixed penalty. For any regime $p$ and baseline $b$, savings are $\Delta X = X_b - X_p$ for $X\in\{M_{loss},E,C,H\}$. The carbon saving $\Delta C$ decomposes exactly into the seven component differences, which we verify to machine precision.

\subsection{A General Decision Rule}
Every term of $C$ is either linear in the defect count $D$ (routing, material, rework, escapes, defect alerts) or independent of it (edge electricity, hardware, false-alert review, manual inspection). For any policy $p$ and baseline $b$, therefore,
\begin{equation}
\Delta C(\pi) = N\pi\,\beta - F, \qquad \pi^\star = \frac{F}{N\beta},
\label{eq:rule}
\end{equation}
where $\beta$ is the net carbon saved per defect and $F$ the fixed carbon per functional unit. For an AI policy against no inspection, $F/N = k$ is the edge cell's carbon per part,
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
k = \frac{1}{\Theta}\Big[&\frac{\gamma(P_{idle}+P_{active}+P_{host})}{1000} + \frac{C_{hw}}{L_{hw}} \\
&+ \frac{\gamma\,\lambda_{FA}\,t_{review}P_{station}}{3.6\times10^{6}}\Big],
\end{split}
\end{equation}
and $\beta = r\,[\,m\,EF_{mat}(1+\kappa f_C)+c_{ret}-h\,]$, where $h$ is the carbon of handling an intercepted defect (scrap and recycling, rework electricity, alert review). Edge AI is carbon-beneficial exactly when $\pi\beta>k$: a defect rate times a per-defect saving must exceed a per-part cost that falls with line throughput. The implementation obtains $\beta$ and $F$ from two model evaluations, so~(\ref{eq:rule}) holds for every parameter set. Every term of $k$ scales as $1/\Theta$, so multiplying by $\Theta$ gives a throughput-free form: with $D_h=\pi\Theta$ defects per hour and $K=k\Theta$ the cell's carbon per hour, edge AI pays back exactly when $D_h\,\beta>K$. Because $\beta$ approaches the embodied carbon of a part as parts get heavier, the rule reads in plain terms: inspect when the defective parts the line produces per hour carry more embodied carbon than the inspection cell emits per hour.

\subsection{Sustainability Quality Index}
For the four dimensions, all non-negative by construction, the bounded sub-indicators are $S_X=(X_b-X_p)/\max(X_b,X_p)\in[-1,1]$ ($S_X=0$ when $X_b=X_p=0$), and $\mathrm{SQI}=\sum_X w_X S_X$ with four stakeholder weight profiles (balanced, material-, carbon- and human-centred). Any scalarisation embeds value judgements, so we also report the share of the whole weight simplex (uniform Dirichlet samples) for which $\mathrm{SQI}>0$.

\subsection{Parameters and Uncertainty}
Tables~\ref{tab:parameters} and~\ref{tab:policies} list all \RegistryEntries{} parameter entries with central value, bounds, unit, provenance class and source; both tables are generated from the ledger file and cannot drift from the code. The alert-policy entries are the means and 95\% bootstrap intervals reported in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}, imported from one pinned revision of its artifact; the review time is centred on its service rate of \PaperAMu{} reviews/h and the glare rate on its assumed \PaperAGlareRate{} bursts/h. Grid intensity is centred on the EU-27 2023 value (0.242~kg/kWh~\cite{ember2024}), with the Indian FY2022--23 weighted average (0.716~kg/kWh~\cite{cea2024}) as upper bound. Material factors come from the ICE inventory~\cite{ice2011} and the International Aluminium Institute~\cite{iai2023}, the battery-module factor from~\cite{ivl2019}, the embodied carbon and lifetime of the edge computer from a manufacturer footprint~\cite{dell2021optiplex}, and freight intensities from the GLEC Framework~\cite{glec2023} with return distances from Eurostat road-freight statistics~\cite{eurostat2026road}. Defect prevalence is anchored in measured scrap rates: visual moulding defects per resin at a production injection-moulding plant (2.5--9.3\%)~\cite{nguyen2004injection} for scenario~A, and the global Li-ion manufacturing scrap rate (7.67\% in 2023, projected 4.34\% by 2030)~\cite{yu2024scrap} for scenario~C; a public semiconductor line reports 104 failures in 1{,}567 units (6.6\%)~\cite{secom2008}. Recycling burdens come from a post-industrial plastics recycling inventory~\cite{ruggeri2025postindustrial}, the electricity use of EU mechanical recycling plants~\cite{jrc2023plastics}, and industrial Li-ion recycling~\cite{machala2025recycling}. Reworkability, rework energy, line throughput and manual-inspection timing remain scenario assumptions. We propagate uncertainty with \MonteCarloDraws{} independent triangular draws on the ledger bounds (seed 42) and rank global sensitivity with partial rank correlation coefficients (PRCC)~\cite{marino2008methodology}, which capture monotone effects, and with first- and total-order Sobol indices, which decompose the variance of $\Delta C$ including interactions (Saltelli and Jansen estimators~\cite{saltelli2010variance} on a scrambled Sobol sequence, 95\% bootstrap intervals). Brent's method solves each break-even frontier ($\Delta C=0$) on a physically bounded interval; where $\Delta C$ does not change sign, we report ``none'' together with that sign.

\section{Edge Inference Power Measurement}
\label{sec:measure}
\subsection{Workload, Platforms and Protocol}
The workload is the PatchCore detector of~\cite{sengar2026paperA}: an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18, layer-2 and layer-3 features pooled to $28\times28\times384$ patch descriptors, exact 1-nearest-neighbour search against a memory bank, and the Gaussian-smoothed maximum as image score, for $224\times224$ RGB frames at batch size~1. The bank is a greedy coreset of $\PaperABank$ real patch features from \BenchFitImages{} good \BenchCategory{} training images, the size used in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}, and the stream cycles through \BenchFrames{} real \BenchCategory{} test frames, good and defective. We measured four cumulative stages: the model alone; plus score thresholding; plus a temporal policy (exponential smoothing, $k$-of-$N$ persistence and cooldown); and the full pipeline with SQLite write-ahead-log event persistence and JSON serialisation. Each stage ran paced at the line rate of \BenchFps~FPS for \BenchWindow~s windows, in \BenchRepeats{} repeats with a seeded random stage order, and a 15~s idle window preceded every repeat. Power was sampled at 20~Hz and integrated over each window; we report the median across repeats, with the minimum and maximum as bounds.

We ran the protocol on two platforms. The primary one is an embedded \JetsonModel{} module (\JetsonLft, TensorRT \JetsonTensorRT, \JetsonPowerMode{} power mode), the class of device typically mounted beside a line. The whole scoring path---backbone, nearest-neighbour search against the bank, bilinear upsampling, Gaussian filter and maximum---is exported as one ONNX graph whose scores match the PyTorch reference to $10^{-6}$ and compiled to a TensorRT engine; every frame is copied to the device and its score copied back. The module's INA3221 monitor reports its total input power (VDD\_IN), which covers CPU, GPU, memory and SoC, so on this platform only the carrier board, camera and lighting enter through $P_{host}$. FP16 is the deployed precision: its scores deviate from the FP32 reference by at most \JetsonPcHalfMaxRelErr\% and every alert decision on the \BenchFrames{} frames is identical. For comparison we also measured FP32 and a second detector, PaDiM~\cite{defard2021padim} (Section~\ref{sec:detector}). The second platform is a workstation GPU (NVIDIA \GpuName{}, PyTorch \TorchVersion{} in FP32, CUDA \CudaRuntime, WSL2), measured with NVML, which observes the GPU only. Every stage window there contains at least \StageReadingsMin{} distinct sensor readings (idle windows at least \IdleReadingsMin). We logged the NVML cumulative energy counter but do not use it: under WSL2 it reported \CounterIdleMinW--\CounterIdleMaxW~W at idle, inconsistent with the power sensor. The workstation GPU also drives the host desktop; windows disturbed by desktop activity remain in the bounds and in the raw data.

\subsection{Results}
Fig.~\ref{fig:energy} shows that the pipeline stages are indistinguishable on the workstation: median total power ranges over \StageSpreadW~W at \BenchFps~FPS. Thresholding, the temporal policy and event logging add no measurable energy, consistent with the sub-millisecond policy step reported in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}. The whole Jetson module runs the full FP16 pipeline at \JetsonFullTotalPower~W, \JetsonFullActivePower~W above its \JetsonIdlePower~W idle, or \JetsonPcHalfFrameMJ~mJ per frame above idle; FP32 costs \JetsonPcFullFrameMJ~mJ and PaDiM \JetsonPdHalfFrameMJ~mJ (FP16) per frame. The workstation GPU alone draws \FullTotalPower~W (\FullActivePower~W above idle, bounds \FullActivePowerMin--\FullActivePowerMax~W), or \WorkstationFrameMJ~mJ per frame, \FrameEnergyRatio{} times the Jetson's. Unpaced, the Jetson reaches \JetsonPcHalfMaxFps~FPS in FP16 and the workstation \FullMaxFps~FPS, so both sustain the line rate with margin; median per-frame latency on the workstation is \FullLatencyMs~ms, comparable to the \PaperAVisionLatency~ms vision stage reported in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}. With the $P_{host}$ allowance the embedded cell draws about \JetsonCellPower~W, of which the module is only \JetsonComputeShare\%: camera and lighting, not inference, dominate its electricity. The workstation cell draws about \WsCellPower~W. On the embedded platform $E_{edge}$ is between \PrecEdgeKWh{} and \HiValEdgeKWh~kWh per FU, depending on how long the line takes to produce one FU, and the edge cell's carbon (electricity and hardware) is \PlatformCarbonRatioMin--\PlatformCarbonRatioMax{} times lower than with the workstation. No conclusion of Section~\ref{sec:results} depends on the platform: $\Delta C$ against manual inspection changes by at most \PlatformDeltaCMax\%.

\section{Detector Operating Points}
\label{sec:detector}
The same detector, fitted per category, provides the recall the accounting needs. To avoid resting it on one benchmark, we evaluate all \DetMvtecCategories{} MVTec~AD categories~\cite{bergmann2021mvtec} and all \DetVisaCategories{} VisA categories~\cite{zou2022visa} (official one-class split), whose multi-instance and PCB images are closer to production imagery, with PatchCore and, as a second detector, PaDiM~\cite{defard2021padim} (ResNet-18 layers 1--3, 100 randomly retained channels, one Gaussian per patch position). For each category and \DetSeeds{} random splits, 60\% of the good training images fit the detector (PatchCore bank: 10\% coreset, \DetBankMin--\DetBankMax{} patches), 20\% calibrate thresholds, and the remaining 20\% join the good test images as nominal evaluation data (at least \DetGoodEvalMin{} images per category); defective test images give per-part recall. Table~\ref{tab:detector} and Fig.~\ref{fig:detector} (left) report the results. PatchCore reaches a median AUROC of \DetPcMvtecAurocMedian{} on MVTec~AD and \DetPcVisaAurocMedian{} on VisA, in line with published results for small backbones~\cite{roth2022patchcore,zou2022visa}, and is more accurate than PaDiM in \DetPcBeatsPdAuroc{} of \DetCategories{} categories (PaDiM: \DetPdMvtecAurocMedian{} and \DetPdVisaAurocMedian). At the 99th percentile of the calibration scores (q99), PatchCore's median recall is \DetPcMvtecRecallMedian{} on MVTec~AD but \DetPcVisaRecallMedian{} on VisA (PaDiM: \DetPdMvtecRecallMedian{} and \DetPdVisaRecallMedian), and over all categories it ranges from \DetRecallMin{} (\DetWorstCategory) to \DetRecallMax{} at false-positive rates of \DetFprMin--\DetFprMax\%. The ledger's detector recall $r_{AI}$ is PatchCore's median over all \DetCategories{} categories, \DetRecallMedian, with the category range as bounds; it is deliberately the recall of a strict, alarm-budget style threshold, and Section~\ref{sec:thresholds} shows how much a carbon-aware threshold recovers. Recall is measured per image, which is conservative for stations that see a part in several frames, and nominal-image counts limit the resolution of false-positive rates to about one percent. PaDiM also costs more energy per frame on the Jetson (\JetsonPdHalfFrameMJ{} vs \JetsonPcHalfFrameMJ~mJ in FP16): on both counts the detector choice matters more than its power draw.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
\subsection{Regime Comparison}
Table~\ref{tab:regimes} and Fig.~\ref{fig:regimes} summarise the six regimes at central parameter values. Relative to manual inspection, the full policy B3 reduces carbon by \PrecRelCarbonReduction\%, \MetalRelCarbonReduction\% and \HiValRelCarbonReduction\% in scenarios A, B and C ($\Delta C=\PrecDeltaCvsLZero$, \MetalDeltaCvsLZero{} and \HiValDeltaCvsLZero~\kgce{} per FU) and reduces unrecovered material ($\Delta M=\PrecDeltaMvsLZero$, \MetalDeltaMvsLZero{} and \HiValDeltaMvsLZero~kg). It uses \emph{more} electricity ($\Delta E=\PrecDeltaEvsLZero$, $\MetalDeltaEvsLZero$ and $\HiValDeltaEvsLZero$~kWh), almost all of it rework electricity: prompt interception keeps defects reworkable that manual end-of-line inspection finds too late. It also needs more operator time than manual inspection ($\Delta H=\PrecDeltaHvsLZero$, $\MetalDeltaHvsLZero$ and $\HiValDeltaHvsLZero$~h), because every alert, including those caused by glare, takes a full review. Without the incident latch the picture changes completely: single-frame thresholding (B0) produces $\rho=\PrecRhoBZero$, \MetalRhoBZero{} and \HiValRhoBZero{}, i.e.\ it would need \PrecReviewersBZero, \MetalReviewersBZero{} and \HiValReviewersBZero{} reviewers. In scenario~A the resulting workstation electricity makes B0 emit more than manual inspection (\PrecCarbonBZero{} vs \PrecCarbonLZero~\kgce{}). B3 stays below one reviewer in scenarios B and C but needs \PrecReviewersBThree{} in scenario~A ($\rho=\PrecRhoBThree$), whose defect rate exceeds the roughly \PaperALoadCross{} defect episodes per hour that~\cite{sengar2026paperA} found one reviewer can absorb.

\caption{Carbon (left) and operator hours (right, logarithmic) of each regime relative to manual end-of-line inspection L0 (dashed line), at central parameter values.}
\label{fig:regimes}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{What Drives the Carbon Benefit}
The waterfall in Fig.~\ref{fig:waterfall} decomposes $\Delta C$ (B3 vs L0). Avoided field escapes contribute \PrecEscapeShare\%, \MetalEscapeShare\% and \HiValEscapeShare\%, followed by avoided unrecovered material; rework electricity is the largest negative term. Edge electricity and amortised edge hardware together amount to \PrecEdgeCarbon, \MetalEdgeCarbon{} and \HiValEdgeCarbon~\kgce{} per FU---\PrecEdgeOfBenefit\%, \MetalEdgeOfBenefit\% and \HiValEdgeOfBenefit\% of the benefit and at most \EdgeShareMax\% of B3's total footprint. The compute side is thus \EdgeBenefitRatioMin{} to \EdgeBenefitRatioMax{} times smaller than the benefit. Recall, and what an escaped defect costs, decide the outcome.

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig4_carbon_waterfall.pdf}
\caption{Decomposition of $\Delta C$ (B3 vs L0) into its seven additive components, as a share of the net benefit; labels give absolute values in \kgce{} per FU. Positive values are savings.}
\label{fig:waterfall}

\subsection{Break-Even Frontiers}
\label{sec:breakeven}
Table~\ref{tab:uncertainty} and Fig.~\ref{fig:breakeven} report where $\Delta C=0$. Against no inspection, the edge cell pays back its electricity, hardware and review carbon once prevalence exceeds \PrecPiStarNZero, \MetalPiStarNZero{} and \HiValPiStarNZero~ppm. Against manual inspection, B3 stays ahead at any prevalence in scenario~A, where its advantage comes from interception timing rather than from recall, and the frontier lies at \MetalPiStarLZero{} and \HiValPiStarLZero~ppm in scenarios B and C. Holding prevalence at its central value, the edge cell could draw up to \PrecCellPowerStar, \MetalCellPowerStar{} and \HiValCellPowerStar~kW---\PrecCellHeadroom{} to \HiValCellHeadroom{} times the measured value---before the benefit over manual inspection vanishes. For scenarios B and C no break-even exists for grid intensities up to 1.5~kg/kWh, above the life-cycle intensity of coal power (median 0.82~kg/kWh~\cite{schlomer2014annex}), so no average or marginal grid factor reverses them. For the lightweight part of scenario~A the advantage over manual inspection vanishes above \PrecGammaStar~kg/kWh, about the Indian grid average and below a coal margin. The detector's recall is the decisive comparison with people: in scenarios B and C manual inspection would win if inspectors found more than \MetalManualRecallStar{} and \HiValManualRecallStar{} of the defects---above the 70--80\% typically reported for human visual inspection~\cite{see2012visual}, yet PatchCore exceeds even the higher of the two in \DetAboveManualStar{} of \DetCategories{} categories at q99. In scenario~A even perfect manual recall leaves the AI regime ahead, because end-of-line discovery comes too late for rework. Net-negative regimes therefore exist---at very low defect rates, below about \PrecPiStarNZero~ppm for the lightweight part against no inspection, on carbon-intensive grids for lightweight parts, and wherever the detector's recall falls below the inspectors'.

\subsection{Uncertainty and Global Sensitivity}
Across \MonteCarloDraws{} draws of all \UncertainParams{} uncertain parameters, B3 beats no inspection in every draw (\PrecMcProbNZero\%, \MetalMcProbNZero\% and \HiValMcProbNZero\%) but beats manual inspection in only \PrecMcProb\%, \MetalMcProb\% and \HiValMcProb\% of draws, with median $\Delta C$ of \PrecMcMedian, \MetalMcMedian{} and \HiValMcMedian~\kgce{} (5th--95th percentiles in Table~\ref{tab:uncertainty}; Fig.~\ref{fig:uncertainty}, left). The reason is the measured spread of detector recall at the q99 threshold, from \DetRecallMin{} to \DetRecallMax{} across categories, around a median just above the manual recall. The 95th percentile of the edge share of B3's footprint is \PrecMcEdgeShareHigh\%, \MetalMcEdgeShareHigh\% and \HiValMcEdgeShareHigh\%. Fig.~\ref{fig:prcc} decomposes the variance of $\Delta C$ ($\SobolBaseRows$ base rows per Sobol matrix). The largest total-order index belongs to \PrecSobolTop{} in scenario~A ($S_T=\PrecSobolTopST$), \MetalSobolTop{} in B ($\MetalSobolTopST$) and \HiValSobolTop{} in C ($\HiValSobolTopST$). First-order effects carry most of the variance; interactions account for \SobolInteractionMin--\SobolInteractionMax\%, so the monotone PRCC ranking (top coefficients $\PrecTopPrcc$, $\MetalTopPrcc$ and $\HiValTopPrcc$) is a fair summary, and its sign gives the direction of each effect. All edge-cell parameters---edge power, host power, hardware embodied carbon and lifetime---have $S_T\le\EdgeSobolMax$ and $|\mathrm{PRCC}|\le\EdgePrccMax$. Grid intensity acts mainly through rework and review electricity, which B3 increases, so its effect on $\Delta C$ is negative and matters most in scenario~A, where little embodied carbon is at stake. Detector recall alone carries $S_T=\RecallSobolMin$--$\RecallSobolMax$: measuring the detector's recall on a line's own defects, and setting its threshold accordingly (Section~\ref{sec:thresholds}), would narrow the uncertainty far more than better compute measurements.

Colour gives the sign of the partial rank correlation (blue: raises $\Delta C$; red: lowers it).}

\subsection{Alert Policy, Workload and the Recall Margin}
B0--B3 share the same edge cell, so differences among them isolate the alert policy. Smoothing alone (B1) removes most false alerts on good parts, but it raises glare alerts, and neither B1 nor persistence without the latch (B2) changes the roughly 150 alerts each defect raises (Table~\ref{tab:policies}); their operator hours differ by at most \BOneBTwoHoursDiffMax\%. The incident latch of B3 collapses repeat alerts to about one per defect. Relative to B0, B3 saves \PrecDeltaHvsBZero, \MetalDeltaHvsBZero{} and \HiValDeltaHvsBZero~operator hours and \PrecDeltaEvsBZero, \MetalDeltaEvsBZero{} and \HiValDeltaEvsBZero~kWh per FU, and $\Delta C=\PrecDeltaCvsBZero$, \MetalDeltaCvsBZero{} and \HiValDeltaCvsBZero~\kgce{}. The Monte Carlo analysis confirms the carbon saving in \PrecMcProbBZero\% and \MetalMcProbBZero\% of draws in scenarios A and B, but only in \HiValMcProbBZero\% in scenario~C, for the reason explained next. Two effects limit it. First, the persistence delay costs reworkability where it decays fast: in scenario~C it loses \HiValDelayMaterialCost~kg of material per FU relative to smoothing alone, so B1 emits \HiValBOneCarbonEdge~\kgce{} (under 0.1\%) less than B3 there; B1, however, needs \HiValReviewersBOne{} reviewers where B3 needs one. Second, any recall that persistence loses turns into field escapes. The companion study measured no such loss, but a deployment may differ, so we solve for the recall loss $\delta_r^\star$ at which B3's advantage over B0 vanishes (Fig.~\ref{fig:uncertainty}, right). In scenario~A no such loss exists: B0's review electricity outweighs any escapes recall could avoid. In scenarios B and C the margin is \MetalRecallLossStar{} and \HiValRecallLossStar{} percentage points. For high-value parts temporal filtering must therefore preserve recall to within a fraction of a point to remain carbon-beneficial; the ledger allows a loss of up to two points, which is why B3 beats B0 in only a minority of scenario-C draws.

\caption{Left: Monte Carlo distribution of $\Delta C$ for B3 vs manual inspection (box: quartiles; whiskers: 5th--95th percentile). Right: $\Delta C$ of B3 vs single-frame thresholding B0 as a function of the recall lost to persistence $\delta_r$; markers show the break-even $\delta_r^\star$.}
\label{fig:uncertainty}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Reviewer Compliance: The Cry-Wolf Risk}
The accounting so far assumes that reviewers keep every truly defective part the cell diverts. Operators, however, learn how reliable alarms are and comply roughly in proportion to that reliability~\cite{bliss1995probability}, although trained controllers can remain largely compliant~\cite{wickens2009false}. In a detect-and-divert cell, non-compliance means releasing a defective part back to the line, where it escapes. We model the released share of true detections as $\omega(1-\mathrm{PPV})$, where PPV is the share of alerts that concern a defect, $\omega=0$ is full compliance (the value used elsewhere in this paper) and $\omega=1$ is full probability matching, and sweep $\omega$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:crywolf}). The latch that makes B3 operationally feasible also lowers its precision on slow lines: each defect now raises about one alert, while glare alerts keep arriving at a fixed rate per hour. B3's PPV is \PrecPpvBThree\% on the fast line of scenario~A but only \MetalPpvBThree\% and \HiValPpvBThree\% in scenarios B and C. (B1 and B2 appear more precise only because they repeat roughly 150 alerts per defect; B0 adds thousands of false alerts per hour and is less precise still.) In scenario~A, B3 stays ahead of manual inspection even under full probability matching; in B and C its advantage vanishes above $\omega^\star=\MetalOmegaStar$ and \HiValOmegaStar. Where alerts are rare and mostly glare, the release decision should therefore not rest on the reviewer's judgement alone: diverted parts should be re-inspected before release, and glare suppression---the gating stage of~\cite{sengar2026paperA}---is worth more than its electricity suggests.

\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig11_cry_wolf.pdf}
\caption{Cry-wolf risk. Left: alert precision (share of alerts on defective parts) of each alert policy. Right: benefit of B3 over manual inspection as reviewers release diverted defects in proportion to alert unreliability, $\omega(1-\mathrm{PPV})$, normalised to full compliance; markers show the break-even $\omega^\star$.}
\label{fig:crywolf}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Carbon-Optimal Detection Thresholds}
\label{sec:thresholds}
Alarm budgets such as ``at most five false alarms per 1{,}000 parts'' are set for operators, not for carbon. For a one-shot station that takes one image per part and diverts it above a threshold, each point of a measured operating curve fixes recall and false-positive rate; the accounting model then gives total carbon, including the review electricity of every false diversion. Fig.~\ref{fig:detector} (right) compares the carbon-optimal threshold with q99 and with the alarm budget over all \OptPairs{} scenario--category pairs. The optimum is never stricter than the budget and is more permissive than q99 in \OptMorePermissive{} pairs, with a median false-positive rate of \OptFprMedian\% against \BudgetFprMedian\% under the budget and up to \OptFprMax\%. Where the detector is weakest the gain is largest: for \OptWorstCategory{} (\OptWorstDataset), raising the false-positive rate to \OptFprWorst\% lifts recall from \OptRecallWorstQ{} to \OptRecallWorstOpt{} in scenario~C; across categories the optimum saves up to \PrecOptSavingMax, \MetalOptSavingMax{} and \HiValOptSavingMax~\kgce{} per FU in scenarios A, B and C. Constraining the threshold to need no more reviewers than q99 already does leaves the saving almost intact on the slower lines: the capped optimum captures \MetalOptSavingCapShare\% and \HiValOptSavingCapShare\% of the attainable saving in scenarios B and C. On the fast line of scenario~A the unconstrained optimum would need up to \PrecOptRhoMax{} reviewers, and the cap retains \PrecOptSavingCapShare\%. At the capped optimum the median recall over all pairs is \OptCapRecallMedian, against \DetRecallMedian{} at q99 and \ManualRecallCentral{} for manual inspection, so a carbon-aware threshold is also what lifts the detector above human recall. Detection thresholds should therefore be tuned against escape and scrap consequences, with the reviewer budget as a constraint rather than as the objective.

\subsection{Generalisation: A Product Population}
To test whether the conclusions depend on the three reference scenarios, we sample \PopSize{} products: every scenario-specific parameter is drawn log-uniformly over an envelope from half the lowest to twice the highest scenario value, the defect-class mix from a Dirichlet distribution, and all other parameters from their ledger bounds. The full policy beats no inspection for \PopWinNZero\% of the products and manual inspection for \PopWinLZero\%. The second figure mirrors the Monte Carlo analysis: products inherit the full measured recall range at q99, so against manual inspection recall again decides. Fig.~\ref{fig:population} (left) shows that the rule~(\ref{eq:rule}) separates winners from losers exactly: every product lies on the side of the line $\pi=\pi^\star$ that its carbon balance predicts. The edge cell's share of the benefit over manual inspection has a median of \PopEdgeShareMedian\% but exceeds 1\% for \PopEdgeShareAboveOne\% of the products and reaches \PopEdgeShareNinetyFive\% at the 95th percentile (Fig.~\ref{fig:population}, right). Compute becomes relevant only where the quality benefit itself is small: light, low-carbon parts with few defects on slow lines. Fig.~\ref{fig:nomogram} turns the rule into a chart a practitioner can read without the model. On the embedded platform at the central grid factor, edge inspection pays back against no inspection once the product of defects per hour and embodied carbon per part exceeds about \NomogramGramsPerHour~gCO$_2$e/h; the three reference scenarios lie two to five orders of magnitude above this line, and a workstation cell or a carbon-intensive grid shifts it by less than a factor of three.

\subsection{Multi-Criteria Index}
Fig.~\ref{fig:sqi} shows the sub-indicators of B3 against L0. Material and carbon improve, whereas electricity ($S_E=\PrecSE$, $\MetalSE$ and $\HiValSE$) and operator time ($S_H=\PrecSH$, $\MetalSH$ and $\HiValSH$) worsen. The balanced SQI is $\PrecSqiBal$, $\MetalSqiBal$ and $\HiValSqiBal$, and it is positive for \PrecSqiRobust\%, \MetalSqiRobust\% and \HiValSqiRobust\% of all possible weightings. A single index hides a genuine conflict: stakeholders who weight electricity or operator time heavily can rank manual inspection higher even though it emits more carbon. We recommend reporting the sub-indicators and the weight-robustness share, not one score.

\section{Discussion}
\emph{Implications.} The compute footprint of edge inspection is not the decision variable. An embedded module at line rate costs \EdgeBenefitRatioMin{} to \EdgeBenefitRatioMax{} times less carbon than the benefit it enables, a workstation GPU with \FrameEnergyRatio{} times the energy per frame changes the outcome by at most \PlatformDeltaCMax\%, and on embedded hardware the camera and lighting draw more power than inference. Against no inspection the case for edge AI is robust and reduces to one comparison of hourly flows: the embodied carbon of the defects a line produces per hour against the roughly \NomogramGramsPerHour~gCO$_2$e/h the cell emits. Against trained inspectors there is no general answer: the decision turns on whether the detector finds more defects than people do and finds them earlier. On curated MVTec~AD imagery PatchCore usually does; on the harder VisA imagery it often does not at a strict threshold, and the carbon benefit becomes a coin toss. Three design choices move the odds. A carbon-aware threshold accepts more false diversions in exchange for recall and, on slow lines, recovers most of the attainable saving without extra reviewers. An incident latch makes review feasible at all, provided persistence loses less recall than the computed margin. And because the latch leaves glare alerts dominating on slow lines, release decisions should be backed by re-inspection rather than left to reviewers who may learn to distrust the alerts. Practitioners should therefore spend their measurement effort on recall under their own defects, on escape consequences and on alert rates---not on inference energy.

\emph{Threats to validity.} (i) Reworkability, rework energy, throughput and manual timing remain scenario assumptions, and prevalence is proxied by scrap rates (Table~\ref{tab:parameters}), and the escape model counts only part replacement, freight and collateral damage, a lower bound that omits customer-side handling. The results are conditional on these choices, and the uncertainty, break-even and population analyses show how the conclusions shift. (ii) The alert rates come from simulated workloads in~\cite{sengar2026paperA}, with synthetic glare and sensor channels; the glare rate is an assumption, and alerts per defect were measured on 2--8~s defect episodes and are applied unchanged regardless of how long a part stays in view. The persistence recall loss is an assumption, which is why we report the recall margin. (iii) The embedded measurement covers the whole module but not the carrier board, camera and lighting, and the workstation measurement covers the GPU only; both gaps enter through $P_{host}$, which leaves the conclusions unchanged even at its upper bound. The workstation GPU also served the host desktop under WSL2, and NVML sensors have documented sampling limitations~\cite{yang2024accurate}; long paced windows, repeats and robust statistics mitigate these effects without removing them. The Jetson's embodied carbon is a model estimate~\cite{halder2025carbon,gupta2022act} for the module alone. (iv) Detector recall and false-positive rates come from two public benchmarks with few nominal test images per category, measured on single images with a ResNet-18 backbone at $224\times224$; production imagery, drift, larger backbones and multi-view stations change them. This is why we report recall over all \DetCategories{} categories rather than a single value, and why the conclusions against manual inspection are stated conditionally on recall. Larger backbones, multi-camera cells or higher frame rates scale $E_{edge}$ proportionally; even a 100-fold increase stays below the frontiers of Fig.~\ref{fig:breakeven}. (v) Reworkability decay, the detect-and-divert architecture, the single-reviewer queue and the replacement-based escape model are simplifications, and rebound effects and end-of-life treatment lie outside the boundary. (vi) We sample parameters independently, ignoring correlations such as that between part mass and material factor.

\section{Conclusion}
With measured inputs---the power of a real PatchCore pipeline on an embedded module and on a workstation GPU, the recall of two detectors on \DetCategories{} categories of two public benchmarks, and measured alert rates of four alert policies---the sustainability of edge AI inspection is decided by quality, not by compute. The edge cell accounts for at most \EdgeOfBenefitMax\% of the benefit, and against no inspection edge AI pays back whenever $\pi\beta>k$, which held for \PopWinNZero\% of \PopSize{} sampled products. Against manual inspection it pays back only when the detector out-recalls people; at a strict threshold that holds in \McProbLMin--\McProbLMax\% of Monte Carlo draws, and detector recall explains most of the uncertainty. Carbon-aware thresholds, an incident latch with a bounded recall loss, and re-inspection of released parts turn this coin toss into a reliable benefit. All code, raw power traces, detector scores, the parameter ledger and the scripts that generate every figure, table and number in this paper are available at \url{https://github.com/sengarutk/sustainable-edge-quality-intelligence} under the MIT license.
